rv.q: Both laugh-out-loud funny and clutch-your-seat tense, Fish makes it impossible not to feel for its beautifully flawed characters.
The result is a comedy with a dark undertow, a portrait of young women discovering both their power and its limits, and a reminder that growing up has always involved venturing into dangerous waters.
The deeper Karya swims, the funnier Fish becomes.

Overall, Fish is asking interesting questions of its characters and leading us to some unexpected places on stage, but I felt responsible for trying to fit too much of the storytelling puzzle together myself.
This is a scathing, prickly comedy intelligently exploring immigration, adolescence, mother-daughter dynamics and the potential ill effects of the Internet.
Fish, Melis Aker's funny and poignant play, is set in London in 2016, where suspicions about immigrants are driving the country ever closer to Brexit.

Fish is hardly a feel-good play, but it merits attention from theatergoers who look to the stage not merely for entertainment but for a deeper engagement with loss, from the intimate wounds of a fractured family to the global consequences of extremism.
The concept of Fish is deeply engaging and utterly unique.
The cast puts plenty of effort into this muddled affair, but can't redeem it.

cn.t: Aker's darkly comic coming-of-age tale about a teen catfishing ISIS to find her missing brother earns mostly positive reviews for its audacious premise, though some critics find the overstuffed plot struggles to balance its many ambitious storylines.

vr.q: I think it's a really interesting new work that I recommend go checking it out.
